items.title: AI, Employee Productivity and Performance: An Integrated ISM–MICMAC and SEM Investigation of the Pathway from Organisational Investment to Individual Output
items.abstract: Organisations have committed substantial capital to artificial intelligence in workforce management without a settled account of why productivity returns arrive so unevenly across employees working in the same firm under the same systems. This study approaches that problem in two stages. Twelve enabling and constraining factors are first extracted from the AI-HRM literature and ordered through interpretive structural modelling (ISM), with the resulting structure classified by driving and dependence power using MICMAC analysis. The hierarchy that emerges places top management commitment and digital leadership at the base and employee productivity and performance at the eighth and final level, with employee trust in AI and AI-related job insecurity occupying a reciprocal middle position that separates organisational investment from employee outcome. The mid-hierarchy portion of that structure is then specified as a measurement model and estimated on 412 employee responses from Indian knowledge-intensive firms using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling. The measurement model fits acceptably and every construct clears conventional reliability and discriminant validity thresholds. Human-AI task complementarity is the strongest proximal predictor of productivity and performance, followed at some distance by trust in AI and by job insecurity, which carries a negative sign. AI governance and reskilling investment have indirect effects, albeit small but reliable, that are passed on through the process of trust. However, job insecurity undermines the complementarity-performance relationship, although the interaction does not contribute much (under one percent) to the explained variance and should be avoided. The two phases imply that investment in artificial intelligence to boost productivity primarily is reshaping jobs and the context in which they exist.

items.title: An Explainable Agentic AI Framework for Distribution System Load Restoration
items.abstract: Distribution system load restoration is a sequential decision-making problem in which restoration actions must maximize served load, prioritize critical loads, and preserve power-flow feasibility. This paper proposes an explainable agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for distribution system load restoration. The proposed framework uses multiple large language model (LLM) agents for planner guidance, strategic plan generation, decision arbitration, memory-based feedback, and explanation generation. Unlike unconstrained LLM-based control, the proposed method restricts agent decisions to feasible restoration actions and evaluates all candidate plans using deterministic AC power-flow feasibility checks. The framework is evaluated on IEEE 33-bus and 69-bus distribution feeders, as well as a larger IEEE 118-bus test case, and compared against reinforcement learning and planning baselines. The results show that the proposed agentic framework achieves better restoration performance while producing structured explanations for operator-facing decision support. A direct comparison with a Single-LLM-Agent baseline further shows that the proposed multi-agent decomposition improves weighted restored load and critical-load recovery compared with a monolithic LLM decision structure.

items.title: Analysis of counterflow-induced congestion propagation in a high-rise office building staircase: evidence from a full-building phased evacuation drill
items.abstract: In high-rise fire emergencies, ascending firefighters must enter the staircase while occupants are still descending—a structurally unavoidable form of bidirectional flow. Counterflow is recognized as a contributor to staircase congestion, but its building-wide propagation has not been quantified from field data. This observational field study analyzes video counts from a full-building evacuation drill at a 22-story office building (≈2,400 participants); the drill was conducted as a phased evacuation, which serves as the observational context. The analysis focuses on a counterflow event during the normal flow period—after phase-related merging had concluded—isolating counterflow effects from merging. A single pedestrian ascending from Floor 1 to Floor 2 was followed by flow disruption across 14 floors (M2–14F); the stop wave satisfying the ≥ 3-s criterion spanned 12 floors (3F–14F). Congestion duration increased with floor height, from 10 s at Floor 3 to a maximum of 38 s at Floor 13, whereas peak density showed no floor-level trend but was uniformly elevated across affected floors, from a normal-flow mean of 1.36 p/m 2 to a congested mean of 2.18 p/m 2 . The apparent congestion front speed over Floors 3–14 was 0.861 m/s, with onset time increasing almost linearly with path distance, indicating a single coherent front; the resolution front advanced at 0.734 m/s, about 15 % more slowly. These findings provide field-based evidence of the floor-by-floor amplification of congestion duration and motivate—as a safety hypothesis requiring further validation—counterflow-aware evacuation planning where firefighter ascent may coincide with occupant descent.

items.title: Are All Instances Equally Explainable? A Study on the Impact of Locality on the Explainability of Automatic Text Classification Tasks
items.abstract: Many machine learning (ML) models still operate as “black boxes”, limiting users’ ability to understand and trust automated decisions. While Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has advanced, most approaches emphasize model mechanisms or explanation strategies, paying little attention to how the structure of the data itself shapes explanation quality. In this work, we explore the role of locality in shaping the perceived explanation quality for Automatic Text Classification (ATC), where locality consists of how instances are positioned relative to neighbors in representation space. We propose a data-centric framework that characterizes locality using two structural factors: (i) the average similarity between an instance and its neighbors and (ii) the entropy of the local class distribution. Based on these factors, we generate explanations grounded in neighborhood structure through locality-based word clouds and compare them to attention-based explanations. Unlike prior work that typically assumes locality inherently improves explainability, our framework systematically investigates explainability as a function of the spatial organization of data representations , while also establishing a principled way to relate local data characteristics to human-perceived explanatory quality. A user study with over 40 participants across two datasets evaluates explanations under criteria of Satisfaction, Completeness, and Trust . Results reveal that instances in highly homogeneous regions (high similarity, low entropy) produce explanations that users consistently rate as clearer and more useful, with statistically significant differences across datasets. These findings highlight the importance of locality as a key factor in explainability, offering insights for the design of explanation strategies in ATC and broader XAI research.

items.title: Associations of managers’ AI literacy with innovative work behavior and work well-being through AI job crafting and psychological needs satisfaction
items.abstract: Learning to use AI is not the same as benefiting from it. As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in knowledge work, its implications are often discussed in contrasting terms—potential productivity gains and risks to well-being—raising the question of whether AI literacy is associated with both performance-related behavior and well-being. Conceptualizing AI literacy as a learnable competence, this study examines how AI literacy is associated with what managers achieve and how they experience their work. Managers here are examined as adult learners whose roles may provide opportunities to apply AI-related competence in their work. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources perspective and Self-Determination Theory, survey data from 322 managers experienced with generative AI were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. AI literacy was positively associated with AI job crafting, and AI job crafting was positively associated with psychological needs satisfaction (autonomy and competence satisfaction). AI literacy, AI job crafting, and psychological needs satisfaction were also significantly associated with innovative work behavior and work well-being, and the proposed indirect associations were statistically significant.

items.title: Attenuated, Not Absent. Trusting Autonomous Systems Tracks Reliability More Closely, With Less Neural Engagement, Than Trusting Humans
items.abstract: Users of autonomous systems and AI assistants decide whether to accept a system’s output, yet whether such active trust decisions engage the same evaluative architecture as trust between people remains unknown. Forty-four participants made trial-by-trial decisions to trust or distrust a human or autonomous system partner during fMRI, with identical prescripted accuracy for both partners across five difficulty levels. Despite equivalent performance, trust in humans exceeded their reliability. At the highest difficulty level, the estimated probability of trusting the human partner was 72% but only 51% for the system, despite both performing at 52% accuracy. Distrust decisions recruited a prespecified performance monitoring network of valuation, salience, social-perceptual and affective regions. On hard trials, this network remained functionally coupled for both partners. Across the task, trust and distrust were discriminable in every component for both, with greater distrust-related activation and discriminability for human partners. Discriminability differences were expressed on hard trials, where partner accuracy was uncertain and trust diverged between partners. These findings indicate that trust in humans and autonomous systems engages a shared evaluative architecture, but that engagement is attenuated during autonomous system interaction. Whereas our earlier passive monitoring study found the P3a to system errors absent with no behavioural difference, an active decision appears to impose a floor of engagement, so that technology-related cognitive economization, a reduction in cognitive and social-affective resources for non-human partners, takes the form of attenuation rather than absence. Alongside this attenuation, trust in the system tracked its reliability without exceeding it.

items.title: Avatars of ourselves: Exploring professional identity with generative AI in business education
items.abstract: Convincing digital copies of professional selves, avatars that look, sound, and respond like a person, have become easier to produce with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). This paper reports work in progress on a postgraduate business subject at an Australian university, in which students explore professional identity by constructing, testing, and questioning AI representations of themselves. In a curriculum-embedded workshop, students choose between two equivalent activities: building an AI avatar from a self-authored knowledge base or writing a structured professional profile. Both ask students to decide deliberately what to share with, and withhold from, an AI system, then to test their representation against simulated professional scenarios before reflection and debrief. Drawing on postdigital perspectives, the design positions GenAI as neither threat nor solution but as a provocation for identity work. Both critical evaluation of technology and self-knowledge matter more when AI can convincingly represent a person. Preliminary findings from this first iteration, drawn from facilitator reflections and de-identified conversation logs, suggest that the pedagogical value of self-representing avatars lies in the critical questioning they provoke, rather than in their technical sophistication. The workshop offers a practical, adaptable model for critical and creative engagement with GenAI and professional identity.

items.title: Balancing Upward and Downward Communication in Multigenerational Workplaces: An Integrative Review and a Generational Variation-Based Communication Equilibrium Model
items.abstract: Organizations must combine clear downward direction with upward employee voice, and the age diversity of contemporary workforces is often presented as making this balance harder to achieve. This article examines that claim through an integrative review of research on organizational communication, employee voice and silence, psychological safety, organizational justice, and generational diversity. The review covers the four cohorts that dominate today's workforce (Baby Boomers, Generation X, Millennials, and Generation Z), considers Generation Alpha prospectively, and sets boundaries for its central constructs: multigenerational workplace, downward and upward communication, communication balance, and communication equilibrium. Searches combined communication-direction, voice, and generation terms, supplemented by citation tracing and targeted searches of African journal platforms; sources were screened against explicit inclusion criteria, synthesized through data reduction, display, comparison, and verification, and each claim was graded as established, supported, or conjectural. Meta-analytic and consensus evidence shows that differences between generational cohorts in work attitudes are small and confounded with age and period effects. The article therefore proposes a Generational Variation-Based Communication Equilibrium Model (CEM), which starts from age diversity but locates its communicative effects in five proximal sources of variation: career stage, hierarchical role, digital access, work arrangement, and cultural orientation. The model specifies one downward condition (directive clarity), two upward conditions (psychological safety and leadership responsiveness), and one bidirectional condition (channel diversity), which together sustain directional balance, a state in which decision-makers act on clear direction and accurate upward information. Five assumptions underpin the model, and equilibrium is maintained by a balancing responsiveness loop that counters a reinforcing spiral of silence. Eight propositions, with indicators, levels of analysis, and evidential status, set out a research agenda that prioritizes designs separating age, period, and cohort effects and theory built from sub-Saharan African organizations, treating their employees as agents of voice rather than deviations from Northern norms.

items.title: Between risk and reform: Learning designers’ experiences of institutional responses to GenAI in assessment
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to reconsider how assessment can remain meaningful, valid and fit for an AI-integrated future. While institutional responses to GenAI are often framed as technical, policy or academic integrity challenges, they are also deeply human organisational change challenges, shaped by competing logics of risk, reform, infrastructure and operational efficiency. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 11 learning designers (LDs) from six Australian and New Zealand universities, the paper addresses the following research question: How do LDs experience and navigate institutional responses to GenAI in assessment in higher education? The analysis identified five interrelated themes: navigating strategic ambiguity and policy lag; mediating compliance-driven and integrity-focused responses; translating GenAI disruption into assessment reform; bridging AI infrastructure and pedagogical practice; and advocating for educational purpose within operational constraints. The paper contributes to current debates on GenAI and assessment by shifting attention from assessment tasks and technologies to the institutional conditions that shape assessment change. It argues that in addition to policy statements and enterprise AI platforms, sustainable responses to GenAI require coordinated professional development, curriculum governance processes enabling timely change, and stronger recognition of LDs as strategic partners whose pedagogical expertise, institutional knowledge and change leadership are central to assessment transformation.

items.title: Beyond association: Causal risk factors for e-scooter injury from a naturalistic riding study
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of shared e-scooter services has introduced a novel public health challenge, with rising injury rates reported globally. Existing epidemiological studies rely largely on retrospective hospital or police records, which lack data on pre-crash mechanisms. While naturalistic studies have begun to fill this gap, they have thus far relied on associational measures that may be biased by confounding. This study aims to quantify the causal effects of rider behavior and environmental factors on e-scooter safety–critical events (SCEs) using a formal causal inference framework. We conducted a case-control analysis within a naturalistic riding study of a public e-scooter service in Gothenburg, Sweden (2022–2023), drawing from 6868 trips. Our analysis included 61 SCEs (cases) and 183 randomly selected control events. We used directed acyclic graphs to identify confounders and applied the parametric g-formula weighted for exposure duration to estimate adjusted risk ratios (RRs) and risk differences. After adjustment, the risk of an SCE increased substantially for single-handed riding (RR = 5.5), riding through an intersection (RR = 3.8), and inexperience (RR = 2.8). Phone use was associated with an approximately threefold increase in risk (RR = 3.1), though this estimate was not statistically significant. Both rider behavior (e.g., inexperience, single-handed riding) and the built environment (e.g., intersections) are significant causal contributors to e-scooter crash risk. These findings provide evidence for a multi-level public health strategy that focuses on novice rider education, infrastructure modifications at intersections, and technological interventions to support riders during their trips.

items.title: Beyond checklists: A relational approach to UDL implementation
items.abstract: Although Universal Design for Learning (UDL) is grounded in principles of inclusion, flexibility, and learner variability, its implementation in higher education can become reduced to procedural or checklist-driven approaches, creating a tension between its human-centred philosophy and institutional practice. This paper adopts a reflective approach to examine the implementation of UDL across selected courses at an Australian university, exploring how shared understandings of inclusive teaching were co-constructed through dialogue between academics and an educational developer. The reflective inquiry suggests that meaningful UDL implementation is less dependent on frameworks than on relational, dialogic engagement through which pedagogical meaning is negotiated in context. At a time when higher education is increasingly shaped by digital technologies and artificial intelligence, the paper argues for re-centring relationships, collaboration, and human judgement as the foundation of meaningful curriculum transformation. In doing so, it positions educational developers as knowledge architects who facilitate the co-construction of inclusive pedagogical practice and offers a relational perspective on UDL implementation that may inform educational developers and academics seeking to implement inclusive curriculum renewal within their own institutional contexts.

items.title: Beyond conversation length: Conversation openings, cognitive engagement, and support orientations in student-AI chatbot interactions
items.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in learning environments, yet sustained interaction does not necessarily indicate cognitively engaged learning. This exploratory study examined how conversation openings related to cognitive engagement levels and the support orientations reflected in student messages during student-AI interactions. Cognitive engagement was classified by an adapted ICAP framework, openings were organised into a descriptive typology, and semantic thematic analysis was conducted on student messages. Openings oriented towards strategy guidance, conceptual explanation, error understanding, and resource review feedback were more often associated with moderate or deep engagement, whereas resource-evaluation openings were often associated with longer interactions despite limited cognitive depth. Semantic patterns revealed overlapping orientations towards questioning, improvement, examples, feedback, and concepts, spanning clarification, answer checking, revision, application, and task-focused support. These findings distinguish interaction persistence from cognitive engagement and suggest that conversation design should support students to articulate their reasoning and co-construct knowledge with AI, rather than prioritising continued interaction alone.

items.title: Beyond graduate attributes: Embedding employability through reflective practice and work-integrated learning
items.abstract: Graduate employability has become a strategic priority across higher education, yet development of employability capabilities often remains fragmented, positioned outside the curriculum through co-curricular activities or graduate attribute frameworks that lack developmental coherence (Jackson & Bridgstock, 2021). This poster asks: how can employability capabilities be scaffolded longitudinally through reflective practice and Work-Integrated Learning to develop professional identity and career resilience in AI-enabled professional contexts? It presents the curriculum design rationale for the Bachelor of Applied Business at UNSW College, commencing October 2026, demonstrating how digital infrastructure, systematic reflection, and authentic workplace learning build career-ready graduates who work critically with emerging technologies. The design positions reflection not as an isolated assessment task but as career development pedagogy, building metacognitive capability, professional identity, and adaptive resilience across three years. This draws on foundational theories of reflective practice (Schön, 1992) and transformative learning (Mezirow, 1991), integrated with contemporary scholarship on professional identity formation (Jackson, 2016, 2017) and career adaptability (Savickas & Porfeli, 2012). The scaffolded architecture moves from foundational self-awareness tasks in Year 1, through applied workplace reflection during industry placements in Year 2, to integrative professional identity synthesis in the Year 3 capstone—providing authentic contexts for capability development throughout the degree. This progression is enabled through Canvas LMS integrated with the Stackle reflective learning platform. Stackle creates a longitudinal ePortfolio where students document reflective entries across all courses, receive structured prompts aligned to developmental focus, and build a cumulative narrative of professional growth. The curriculum embeds industry engagement through industry-informed assessment tasks across 100% of courses, formal placements, and a capstone industry project. Reflective practice is explicitly connected to each WIL experience through Stackle, requiring students to analyse workplace challenges and articulate capability development—an approach shown to strengthen pre-professional identity formation (Jackson, 2017; Trede et al., 2012). The platform enables integrated feedback from academic supervisors and industry mentors, making capability development visible to students, educators, and potential employers. Embedding AI fluency as a professional capability is central to this design. Rather than treating generative AI as peripheral or threatening to assessment integrity, the curriculum positions AI literacy as essential to contemporary professional practice. Students engage with transparent AI disclosure practices in reflection, use AI tools critically to analyse workplace data, and develop ethical reasoning frameworks for AI use. Assessment structures centre human judgment and applied problem-solving—reflective analysis, workplace challenge responses, and professional presentations—requiring critical thinking about AI outputs rather than uncritical acceptance. This responds to contemporary debates about authentic assessment in AI-mediated learning environments (Bearman et al., 2023), positioning graduates as professionals who work with AI critically and ethically. This poster presents: (1) the theoretical framework; (2) the three-year reflective practice progression model; (3) the WIL integration strategy with 100% industry-informed assessment; and (4) design principles for embedding AI fluency. The contribution is a replicable framework for embedding employability longitudinally while leveraging digital infrastructure to support human agency in AI-augmented professional contexts.

items.title: Beyond permission: Mapping generative AI policy approaches across Australian universities
items.abstract: Australian universities are revising generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) guidance under strong pressure to assure learning, academic integrity and assessment quality. This concise paper reports a public-source mapping of GenAI policy, assessment guidance and student AI-literacy preparation across the 38 Universities Australia member universities. Using six TEQSA sources as contextual material, 100 university sources were coded by authority level, dominant public guidance approach, assessment model and student-facing literacy support. The public evidence shows diverse policy configurations: 18 universities used a structured framework, scale, tier or lane model, while eight relied mainly on assessment-specific rules. Student preparation was also prominent: 19 universities provided formal AI-specific learning opportunities, and 12 provided structured student hubs or toolkits. The findings suggest that GenAI policy can function as curriculum infrastructure rather than only academic-integrity compliance. The paper contributes to Human-Centred Learning Design by treating GenAI policy as learning design infrastructure that connects assessment authority, student trust, feedback expectations and AI literacy.

items.title: Beyond prompting: An epistemic agency framework for generative AI literacy
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has fundamentally altered how learners access, construct, and engage with knowledge. Existing discussions of GenAI literacy have largely emphasised operational competencies, such as prompt engineering, understanding AI capabilities, and ethical use. While these competencies remain important, they do not fully address the epistemic challenges arising from AI-mediated knowledge production. This paper proposes reframing GenAI literacy through the lens of epistemic agency; that is, learners’ capacity to critically evaluate, regulate, justify, and take responsibility for knowledge generated in collaboration with intelligent systems. Rather than viewing GenAI literacy as a collection of technical skills, this conceptual paper argues that its primary educational purpose is to cultivate learners who can exercise informed judgement in increasingly AI-mediated learning environments. Building on existing AI literacy scholarship and theories of epistemic agency, the paper introduces a conceptual framework comprising four interrelated dimensions: epistemic evaluation, epistemic regulation, epistemic responsibility, and epistemic autonomy. The framework provides a theoretically grounded perspective for understanding how GenAI literacy can move beyond operational competence towards fostering independent, reflective, and responsible knowledge construction.

items.title: Beyond the pretty graph: Human-centred assessment design for evaluative judgement
items.abstract: Assessment in data visualisation courses too often rewards technical output over communicating substance. When visualisation is taught as a tool rather than a discipline, students learn to produce work that meets the brief but has little to say. This paper reports on a course redesign that addresses this gap through a human-centred assessment design grounded in evaluative judgement theory, treating evaluative judgement as a capability exercised by both students and markers. The redesign is structured around five elements addressing student ownership of project topics, portfolio assessment, descriptive capability levels, practitioner modelling, and creative freedom within a structured framework, implemented in a required course within a Master of Data Science program. Practitioner inquiry into the operation of this design in the presence of generative AI revealed that AI functioned not as a threat to academic integrity but as a mechanism that raised creative ambition, shifting the limiting factor from technical skill to evaluative judgement. Although situated in a data visualisation course, the contribution is broader. As generative AI makes technical production easier, helping students develop the capacity to recognise, justify, and communicate insight becomes the central challenge across higher education, and this paper suggests one way to address it.

items.abstract: The rapid growth of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has accelerated institutional investment in AI infrastructure, yet many universities continue to face difficulties translating institutional strategy into consistent subject-level teaching practice. The paper reports the design rationale, outputs and approved deployment model of the framework, including staff capability resources, configurable AI templates, disclosure mechanisms and governance processes. Informed by Educational Design Research and scholarship on organisational change in education, the paper argues that Schools can serve as meso-level environments that enact institutional AI strategy through resources and structures designed to support subject-level teaching practice. It contributes a meso-level governance model, six transferable design principles, and an operational framework intended to support responsible and human-centred AI-supported learning. items.title: Bridging the articulation gap: A multi-agent conversational AI platform for compassionate scaffolding of technical interview skills
items.abstract: Technical job interviews place computing students under pressure to demonstrate algorithmic and communication skills simultaneously under live observation, producing what we term the articulation gap. Existing preparation pathways provide only partial support: coding platforms ignore communication, coaching is economically inaccessible, and current AI simulators remain reactive. We present AIView, a multi-agent conversational platform that scaffolds integrated interview competencies. A LangGraph orchestrator coordinates specialised agents for question delivery and adaptive guidance alongside verbalisation monitors and an affect-aware tone layer, with assessments anchored in the SOLO taxonomy. An evaluation with 31 students showed high usability (SUS = 73.8), strong trust in AI feedback (M = 3.94), and high recommendation intent (M = 4.29). Participants valued personalised, code-aware feedback and a low-pressure learning environment. By fostering compassionate human-AI collaboration that supports creative problem solving and connection in a digital learning environment, AIView represents a step towards democratising access to career preparation through adaptive scaffolding.

items.title: Building creativity with generative AI through reflective practice
items.abstract: Generative AI poses a risk to students’ creative thinking when it is adopted without critical reflection (Elgammal, 2026). These tools are marketed as collaborators and tutors, offering constant and largely uncritical encouragement (Chow & Celis Bueno, 2025; Walsh 2025). This presentation holds the promise of AI partnership alongside evidence that these tools displace cognitive and creative effort (Gerlich, 2025; Temler 2026). This problem is widely recognised, but proposed responses remain inconsistent, vague or untested. Many calls to address the use of generative AI correctly identify the problem or alternatively show singular approaches and case studies. What is needed is a discipline-agnostic framework on building students’ awareness of their own creative processes in the context of these tools. The approach offered here to develop creativity with AI has two theoretical foundations: Margaret Boden’s theory of creativity and art, and the Kolb Experiential Learning Cycle (2011) as a pedagogical approach. Boden (2004 distinguishes combinational, exploratory and transformational creativity: the recombination of existing ideas, movement within a conceptual space, and alteration of that space’s defining dimensions. Novelty can be either new to the individual or new more generally under this view. Boden argues that novelty may come about in several ways, including combining existing ideas in new ways, exploring or changing existing ideas, or transforming dimensions of those ideas. The two frameworks do different work. Boden supplies the criteria students apply when judging whether their output is genuinely novel, surprising and valuable; Kolb supplies the cycle through which that judgement is made repeatedly and acted upon. Without Boden, reflection has no object; without Kolb, the criteria are applied once and forgotten. Students work through Kolb’s (2011) four stages in their learning: concrete experience, reflective observation, abstract conceptualisation, and active experimentation. These each serve a cumulative purpose in developing the students’ collaborative process with generative AI. In the first phase, the student does their first draft of a creative process, using AI in any way they want to experiment with. Afterward, they reflect on that experience, considering questions about what skills they developed (or did not), whether the draft did what they wanted it to do, and how they felt about the AI tool use. Based on this reflection, they can then develop and express a personal set of beliefs on practical use of generative AI. Finally, they can try out a new approach based on these conclusions – which then become the next concrete experience. It is an ongoing and cyclical process of practical experimentation and personal reflection. The framework is adapted from the “Creativity and AI” module of Sage’s Digital Literacy course (Zaphir & Henrickson, in press). Its purpose is to be discipline agnostic; a framework which can be broadly applicable across cohorts and disciplines. Critical AI literacies require the development of students’ own ethical ideas and practical skills in using the tools; this process is designed to be adaptable in any context. Creativity has different implications and different applications in each discipline. AI can act as a useful collaborator if the user can state what and why they want to do it. Students will all benefit in the exercise of deliberately choosing which skills to offload and which to augment, and then reflecting on their choices with each use. The presentation works through one complete turn of the cycle using a worked example: the initial AI-assisted draft, the reflective prompts applied to it, the position statement the student produced, and the changed approach taken on the next attempt. Slides alternate between student artefacts and the framework stage they illustrate. Attendees will leave with the reflection prompts used at each stage and a one-page cycle template they can adapt to their own discipline and cohort.

items.title: Can GenAI numeracy tutors support self-regulated learning?
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been the focus of much attention in the higher education sector, both for its potential to support personalised and adaptive learning, but also due to the risk that students may outsource learning to it, leading to gaps in their professional or discipline competencies. This risk of cognitive offloading applies equally to learning how to learn, a skill set explored through studies of self-regulated learning (SRL). Two GenAI numeracy tutors were piloted at a regional Australian university as one component of a newly launched mathematics and statistics support centre, one focusing on medication calculations for Nursing students (NiNA), and the other on threshold numeracy skills for Education students (EdNA). Detailed analysis of students’ conversations with these agents using Zimmerman and Moylan’s 2009 SRL framework revealed extensive evidence of some elements of SRL such as strategic planning, task-specific strategies, and adaptive competence; trace evidence of other elements including self-efficacy and self-evaluation; and no evidence of the remaining elements. This study contributes an underrepresented qualitative perspective to the body of research into the crossover of GenAI and SRL and foreshadows avenues for further research and refinements in the design of GenAI numeracy tutors.

items.title: CATALOGAÇÃO ASSISTIDA POR INTELIGÊNCIA ARTIFICIAL EM AMBIENTE REAL: EFICIÊNCIA, COMPLETUDE E SOBERANIA TÉCNICA DO BIBLIOTECÁRIO
items.abstract: Esta pesquisa analisou a incorporação de um módulo multimodal de inteligência artificial (IA), o Acelerador de Catalogação, a um sistema de gestão de bibliotecas, com objetivo central de considerar o impacto dessa ferramenta na rotina de processamento técnico, avaliando a eficiência operacional, a precisão da extração de dados e a facilidade de uso, com especial atenção à preservação da soberania técnica do bibliotecário. Realizou-se um estudo de caso quali-quantitativo em ambiente real de trabalho, com 12 bibliotecários voluntários experientes em catalogação tradicional. Os dados quantitativos, extraídos automaticamente pelo sistema, compararam 52 registros do regime tradicional e 64 do regime assistido por IA; os dados qualitativos vieram de um fórum de diálogo colaborativo, contido como ferramenta do próprio software com recursos de interação e engajamento, este fórum foi subdividido em cinco eixos temáticos, tratado por análise de conteúdo. Os resultados evidenciaram uma redução média por título que caiu 32,5% (de 10 min 13 s para 6 min 54 s) e a completude aumentou 24,5% (de 23,6 para 29,4 campos preenchidos). A IA foi eficaz em tarefas mimeomórficas (ações mecânicas, repetitivas e estruturadas), enquanto as tarefas polimórficas, que exigem julgamento contextual, tratamento de exceções e adequação a políticas locais, permaneceram com o profissional, porém com sugestões do agente de IA. Observou-se maior incidência de edições posteriores ao cadastro no regime assistido (11 em 64 processos, contra 2 em 52), concentrada em um catalogador e em obras jurídicas. Os participantes descreveram a tecnologia como “assistente sob comando”, o que sustenta a curadoria humana como componente estrutural do fluxo. Concluiu-se que o ganho de eficiência convive com a preservação da autoridade técnica e do protagonismo do bibliotecário.

items.title: Caught in the algorithm: Student discourse on AI governance, surveillance, and academic integrity in higher education
items.abstract: This study examines how awareness of generative AI academic integrity policies shapes student anxiety, ethical reasoning, and writing practices in higher education. Drawing on a reflexive thematic analysis of student discourse from YouTube and Reddit, the study explores how detection-oriented governance frameworks are experienced and negotiated outside formal institutional contexts. Findings indicate that students do not primarily describe intentional rule-breaking; instead, they articulate experiences of surveillance, uncertainty, and adaptation within assessment systems perceived as inconsistent and adversarial. Three interrelated themes are identified: surveillance anxiety and defensive authorship; normative dissonance and moral negotiation of AI use; and cognitive offloading, systemic strain, and declining trust in assessment integrity. Across these themes, AI policy awareness is shown to shape not only behavioural responses but also students’ affective and epistemic relationships with writing, authorship, and institutional authority. The study argues that detection-first approaches risk intensifying anxiety and undermining trust without resolving underlying tensions in assessment design. It concludes that generative AI exposes structural fragilities in higher education, suggesting the need to reorient academic integrity governance toward design-led, transparent, and equity-sensitive approaches that prioritise learning, trust, and student experience.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Characterising human cognitive security and its behavioural outcomes within an integrative modelling framework
items.abstract: Human decision-making under uncertainty faces growing challenges from information-based threats that pose risks to human cognitive processes and behaviour. Although their potential harm is widely acknowledged, there remains no well-defined construct for characterising the degree to which information-based threats influence changes in human judgments and decision-making, impeding theoretical advancement, measurement, and effective countermeasure development. Here, we introduce a human cognitive security construct focused on linking information-based threats to observable outcomes to bridge field-level definitions with operational measures by drawing from core mechanisms related to information processing and decision-making. To connect the information environment to behaviour, we develop an integrative modelling framework that unifies Bayesian inference with affect-modulated decision valuation, capturing how cognitive resource allocation and affective valuation shape three core behavioural outcomes: veracity discernment, task-oriented actions, and information sharing. Through computational simulations, we demonstrate that this framework can explain canonical phenomena, including cognitive heuristics and incongruent veracity discernment and sharing behaviour, and we test model predictions against empirical data of the illusory truth effect (R² = 0.86). To guide future empirical examinations, we propose empirically grounded behavioural outcome measures of cognitive security and outline how environment-specific elements, characterised by data availability and ecological constraints, affect individuals’ cognitive security.

items.title: Classification AI vs Generative AI in grading and feedback
items.abstract: Marking is among the most time-consuming activities in education, and artificial intelligence (AI) is widely proposed as a remedy. Attention has centred on generative large language models, yet regulators raise concerns about their bias, consistency, and explainability. This paper contrasts generative grading with per-question classification models trained only on an educator’s own marking and deployed in a human-in-the-loop workflow. The architectures are compared against criteria drawn from regulatory guidance: transparency, construct-relevant features, determinism, and specifiable training data. A narrower role for generative models is also identified, in composing and restructuring marker-approved feedback rather than in marking. Deployment analytics from one platform are then reported, covering approximately 166,000 marked questions, 39,500 essays, and six institutions: 66.2% of questions were marked in under one minute, 77.6% to 89.5% of AI suggestions were accepted, and essay models reached a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.93 for high-confidence predictions. Questionnaire responses from earlier pilots (33 markers, 30 students) are also reported: markers described marking as faster and consistent feedback as easier to provide; most students rated feedback more consistent and higher in quality. Implications for institutions selecting or building such tools are discussed, alongside the limitations of vendor-collected data.

items.title: Cogniti agents in practice: AI as academic infrastructure in a foundation business course
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly entering universities not only as a student-owned productivity tool but as part of the digital infrastructure through which learning support, feedback and assessment guidance are mediated. This concise paper reports on an exploratory pilot of Cogniti AI agents in an Aotearoa New Zealand foundation business course, with a focus on human-centred learning design. The pilot involved five role-specialised agents: a course buddy for administration support, a case-discussion agent for Maori entrepreneurship learning, and three virtual team members focused on task coordination, relationship management and value-adding contribution. Rather than positioning AI as a generic chatbot, the paper presents a design model for embedding AI agents within the course ecosystem. Drawing on design records, early usage patterns and practice reflections, the paper argues that AI agents can extend human-centred pedagogy when they are co-created with students, shaped by student input, assessment-aligned, and circumscribed by teacher oversight. The contribution is a practical model for integrating AI agents into learning management systems in ways that prioritise connection, mentorship, evaluative judgement, feedback literacy and collaborative learning.

items.title: Comparing the positive and negative impacts of AI: A large-scale study of student perspectives
items.abstract: Higher education students are incorporating generative artificial intelligence into many aspects of their studies, yet the ways they judge its positive and negative impacts remain poorly understood. Using qualitative content analysis supported by code-frequency analysis, this paper examines open-ended comments from 2,802 participants drawn from a survey of 8,021 students across four Australian universities. Reported impacts clustered around four themes: study practices, quality, efficiency, and institutional practices. Positive impacts were more frequently coded overall, particularly when students described using AI to support their own study practices and efficiency. Negative responses centred on the inaccuracy of AI outputs. Although relatively few participants commented on institutional teaching and assessment practices, these responses were predominantly negative. The findings suggest that students value AI not only for the quality of its outputs, but also for its role in helping them begin, continue, refine, and complete academic work. Rather than uncritically accepting or categorically rejecting AI, students appeared to make situated judgements about its usefulness and limitations, shaped by concerns about accuracy and trust, as well as by the agency and control they retained over its use. Institutional responses should therefore engage with the complexity of students’ practices and the conditions under which they perceive AI to be useful or problematic.

items.title: Compassionate AI by design: Reconnecting students with learning through course-tailored AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is becoming part of students’ everyday study practices, yet institutional debate still tends to position it as either an efficiency tool or an academic-integrity threat. This binary framing obscures a more educationally useful question: can AI be designed to help students engage meaningfully with difficult concepts while helping educators see where understanding breaks down? This project evaluates a course-tailored AI learning assistant embedded in a large undergraduate course at an Australian public university. The tool was bounded to authoritative course materials and instructor-provided resources. Students could ask questions, receive course-grounded answers and explanations, and clarify or organise their understanding without having assessed tasks completed for them. Informed by self-determination theory and cognitive load theory, the design sought to support competence and autonomy, reduce unnecessary cognitive burden, and provide low-stakes help at the moment of uncertainty (Ryan & Deci, 2000; Sweller, 1988). Students were randomly assigned either access to the tool or standard course resources. Evaluation drew on complementary sources of evidence gathered across the teaching period, combining students’ own accounts of their experience with routinely captured indicators of engagement and achievement. The evidence points in a consistent direction. Students with access reported a more positive orientation towards their study and towards the responsible institutional use of AI. Their engagement shifted in character rather than in volume, suggesting sustained attention to core course materials rather than a general increase in undifferentiated digital activity. Indications for achievement were encouraging, particularly for students at greater risk of not succeeding, although the strength of these signals varied. An equally important feature lay in the questions themselves. Patterns in students’ questions made recurring misconceptions and points of uncertainty more visible to the educator. This supported more responsive teaching: explanations, examples, and follow-up support could be focused on what students were actually struggling to understand. The initiative therefore created a two-way pedagogical feedback loop. Students received immediate, course-aligned support for working through concepts, while the educator gained diagnostic insight into learning needs not always visible in conventional analytics or classroom participation. The project locates compassion in the design choices, not in the technology itself. Course alignment, bounded assistance, student choice, and attention to digital burden offer a way for AI to support conceptual engagement without displacing core resources or student agency (Burr et al., 2020; Holmes et al., 2022). The resulting principles are to ground AI in authoritative course materials, preserve the integrity of assessed work, enable low-stakes questioning, use question patterns to inform teaching, and evaluate wellbeing alongside engagement and achievement. These principles are applicable across disciplines and tertiary contexts.

items.title: Computer-Gamified Pedagogy in English Vocabulary Teaching
items.abstract: To address the problems of decontextualized vocabulary drills and the lack of adaptive, data-informed instruction, this study designs and evaluates a web-based gamified vocabulary system integrating an adaptive task sequencing algorithm, real-time learning analytics, and multimodal scenarios within a constructivist framework. In a 16-week quasi-experiment with 200 non-English-major undergraduates, the experimental group (n = 100) improved by 22.5 points in total vocabulary score, in comparison with an improvement of 11.3 points in the control group (n = 100), with the largest gains made in low-frequency word mastery (+41.5%) and vocabulary application (+39.6%). The experimental group also reported higher intrinsic motivation (4.32 vs. 3.56, p < .001), and platform logs showed task completion rising from 78.6% to 93.8% and error rate falling from 28.4% to 10.1%. Two teachers used the dashboard for data-informed instructional adjustments. These findings illustrate how web-based learning technologies can support learner autonomy and instructional decision-making in higher education.

items.title: Concisely Explaining the Doubt: Minimum-Size Abductive Explanations for Linear Models with a Reject Option
items.abstract: Trustworthiness in artificial intelligence depends not only on what a model decides, but also on how it handles and explains cases in which a reliable decision cannot be made. In critical domains such as healthcare and finance, a reject option allows the model to abstain when evidence is insufficient, making it essential to explain why an instance is rejected in order to support informed human intervention. In these settings, explanations must not only be interpretable, but also faithful to the underlying model and computationally efficient enough to support real-time decision making. Abductive explanations guarantee fidelity, but their exact computation is known to be NP-hard for many classes of models, limiting their practical applicability. Computing minimum-size abductive explanations is an even more challenging problem, as it requires reasoning not only about fidelity but also about optimality. Prior work has addressed this challenge in restricted settings, including log-linear-time algorithms for computing minimum-size abductive explanations in linear models without rejection, as well as a polynomial-time method based on linear programming for computing abductive explanations, without guarantees of minimum size, for linear models with a reject option. In this work, we bridge these lines of research by computing minimum-size abductive explanations for linear models with a reject option. For accepted instances, we adapt the log-linear algorithm to efficiently compute optimal explanations. For rejected instances, we formulate a 0–1 integer linear programming problem that characterizes minimum-size abductive explanations of rejection. Although this formulation is NP-hard in theory, our experimental results show that it is consistently more efficient in practice than the linear-programming-based approach that does not guarantee minimum-size explanations.

items.title: Controlling Proactive Multimodal AI: Separating Perception from Participation
items.abstract: Proactive multimodal AI can watch a user's screen, listen to speech, track interaction, and decide whether to enter unfolding work. Little is known about how people want to control what such AI may perceive and how far it may participate. Informed by a 14-person Wizard-of-Oz study, we built SpotMe, a design probe that senses screen, speech, and interaction; chooses Silence, Ask, or Assist; and lets users separately configure what it may perceive, how far it may participate, and what types of support it may provide. In a 16-person study on a civic dashboard, participants first experienced proactive help, then inspected decisions to act or remain silent, and then configured SpotMe's perception and participation. We found that participants could keep all perception channels available while lowering participation to Ask or Silence; that exposing suppressed decisions made silence interpretable and contestable; and that seeing what SpotMe used led some to change how they clicked, highlighted, and spoke. We contribute an empirical account of inspecting and controlling proactive multimodal AI by decoupling perception from participation.

items.title: Conversational pedagogy in practice: Exploring a unit-embedded GenAI chatbot in higher education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) chatbots are increasingly being adopted in higher education; however, limited research has examined their pedagogical integration within learning environments. This paper reports findings from an exploratory mixed-methods case study of a GenAI chatbot embedded in a postgraduate unit at an Australian university. Designed as a pedagogically embedded learning companion, the chatbot provided contextualised guidance and functioned as a first point of contact for students seeking clarification and support. Findings indicate that students perceived the chatbot as a useful and accessible learning resource that supported engagement, reflection, and self-directed learning. Three themes emerged: first-contact pedagogical support, AI-mediated scaffolding, and human-AI complementarity. Students valued the immediacy and contextual relevance of responses while recognising the continuing importance of educator guidance. These initial findings provide insights into the design of pedagogically embedded GenAI learning companions and their potential role in supporting learning within higher education.

items.title: Designing AI-mediated interactive learning environments for communication skills: Insights from two implementations
items.abstract: Developing communication skills remains a core challenge in higher education, particularly in providing scalable opportunities for practice and feedback. This study explores how artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated systems function as interactive learning environments for communication skills development. Two implementations are examined: a voice-only conversational AI-mediated system used across health disciplines and a digital human avatar used in a business unit. A mixed-methods design was employed, combining quantitative survey data and qualitative content. Findings highlighted three key affordances: repeated low-stakes practice, immediate feedback, and flexible engagement. Students reported increased confidence and perceived skill development. Limitations included conversational inaccuracies, realism, technical reliability, and feedback consistency. Importantly, findings indicate that the effectiveness of AI systems is strongly influenced by prompt design, scenario construction, and alignment with learner level. This paper reframes AI tools not as autonomous technologies, but as designed interactive learning environments requiring careful pedagogical integration. Implications are discussed for the design of AI-supported learning activities, particularly in contexts involving oral communication and authentic assessment.

items.title: Designing assessment through transformation: A learning beyond the classroom approach to AI-mediated assessment
items.abstract: Where does meaningful learning begin in an era of generative artificial intelligence (AI)? Current responses to AI in higher education have largely focused on assessment redesign, academic integrity and AI literacy. While these developments have strengthened assessment practice, they often assume that meaningful learning begins when students enter university. This paper argues that responding effectively to AI requires reconsidering this assumption. Drawing upon the learning beyond the classroom framework, it proposes assessment through transformation as a philosophy for assessment design that recognises learners’ existing educational resources and supports their development into disciplinary judgement. This paper contributes in three ways. First, it introduces the learning beyond the classroom framework as a conceptual foundation for understanding learning in AI-mediated higher education. Second, it proposes assessment through transformation as a philosophy that connects recognition, translation, transformation and disciplinary judgement within a developmental approach to assessment design. Third, it translates this philosophy into five practical principles that provide educators with a flexible lens for redesigning assessment across diverse disciplinary contexts. Rather than treating AI as the central educational challenge, the paper positions it as a catalyst for reconsidering the purposes of assessment, arguing that higher education’s enduring contribution lies in cultivating critical judgement, ethical reasoning and meaningful contribution.

items.title: Designing authentic learning through anchor scenarios: A whole-of-unit approach
items.abstract: In technology disciplines, students are more engaged and better prepared for employment when they experience technical work as purposeful professional practice rather than as isolated exercises (Kerven et al., 2017). Generative AI can now produce working code, configured systems and polished documentation, so students can complete tasks that mainly ask for these outputs without doing much of the work themselves. Such tasks are unlikely to hold students’ interest, and the work submitted can be weak evidence of capability. The professional judgement remains theirs: deciding what should be built, for whom, within which constraints, and with what consequences. The challenge for curriculum design is to integrate, teach and assess that judgement. This presentation describes a curriculum design we developed in response. Each unit is set in one authentic workplace context, the anchor scenario, which defines the stakeholders, constraints and outcome for the whole unit. Every session then presents a session scenario: a professional decision in that context, building on the one before. In the final assessment, students deliver the outcome the anchor scenario set. Content is taught when students need it for a decision, and assessment is set in the same context. The approach draws on situated learning, in which judgement develops through authentic activity in realistic contexts (Brown et al., 1989; Lave & Wenger, 1991), and on Action Mapping, which begins from a real workplace outcome and derives the decisions learners must make before selecting content (Moore, 2017). Narrative carries more force when scenarios accumulate rather than stand alone (Bruner, 1991). Sustained scenario structures have precedents: anchored instruction centres on one extended problem (Cognition and Technology Group at Vanderbilt, 1990), media computation organises content coverage (Guzdial, 2003), and task-driven case studies guide practice rather than judgement (Porubän et al., 2024). None spans an entire unit while structuring cumulative professional decisions, producing employer-facing artefacts, and giving AI a purposeful role. Each unit is built in three phases. The Anchor phase derives the scenario from a workplace outcome and produces a unit design plan mapping outcomes to assessments and giving every session its own scenario. The Embed phase scripts each session in full, writing assessments at the same time and checking alignment in both directions (Biggs, 1996), with every activity carrying a short connection back to the scenario. The Shift phase builds the design as web-based learning paths for delivery on campus, online or in hybrid mode. This approach now runs in more than 30 units across five discipline areas.
